name: New Confucianism
summary: New Confucianism (Modern Confucianism) is a twentieth-century Chinese philosophical movement, centred on Xiong Shili's followers Mou Zongsan, Tang Junyi and Xu Fuguan and their 1958 Manifesto on Chinese culture, that defends Confucian moral metaphysics against wholesale Westernization and Marxism. It holds that Chinese culture must develop science and democratic constitutional government out of its own moral foundations: every person is an equal moral and political subject, so monarchy and one-party dictatorship are rejected and power should change hands through free elections under a constitution. It condemns communism as a denial of universal human nature and freedom, criticizes imperialism and the spiritual emptiness of modern Western culture, and upholds filial piety, cultural continuity and a non-dogmatic Confucian religiosity tolerant of all faiths.
scope: As the defining scholarship sets it out: the SEP entry on Modern Confucianism (s1) says New Confucianism 'specifically usually refers to' Xiong Shili's followers Mou Zongsan, Tang Junyi and Xu Fuguan and their followers, and names their 1958 'New Confucian Manifesto' (co-signed with Zhang Junmai) as the movement's watershed; Sernelj (s2, s9) and the IEP entry on Mou (s4) describe the same second-generation group. The profile is answered from the Manifesto's Chinese text (s7), the SEP and IEP entries, Sernelj's studies of the Manifesto and of Xu Fuguan, and Fröhlich's study of Tang Junyi (s8). Where the three thinkers differ, the answer says so. Jiang Qing's mainland 'political Confucianism' and Confucian meritocracy are excluded: the SEP presents Confucian meritocracy as a later anti-democratic view the New Confucians 'would have rejected'. Classical Confucianism and Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism are other subjects. The movement never governed, so it has no record of its own and every answer rests on its words.

keyFigures.role: Leading second-generation philosopher; argued that Confucian morality must 'restrict itself' to give rise to science and democracy

keyFigures.name: Tang Junyi
keyFigures.role: Main drafter of the 1958 Manifesto; philosopher of the moral heart-mind and of a Confucian basis for democracy

keyFigures.name: Xu Fuguan
keyFigures.role: Co-author of the 1958 Manifesto and the movement's most political thinker, a critic of both communism and Nationalist rule

missingStatements.text: Democratic institutions are needed but must be grounded in a shared moral vision of the person rather than treated as morally neutral procedures.
missingStatements.rationale: Mou held democracy is not itself a moral system yet requires moral foundations, and Tang held democracy needs a vision of persons as moral beings while rejecting purely political liberalism.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-09), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-19) leaned on Wikipedia (s3, s5, s6) and treated Jiang Qing's political Confucianism as a dissenting branch; the SEP (s1) instead sets Confucian meritocracy apart from New Confucianism, so answers resting on Jiang Qing were nulled, and every other first-pass answer was checked against the sources and kept, changed or nulled, with the first version kept in each statement's reviewHistory. This pass read in full the Manifesto (s7, Chinese text), the SEP and IEP entries, Sernelj's chapter and article, and the political chapters of Fröhlich's study of Tang (chs. 1, 8-10, 12). Themes searched: government and democracy (Manifesto sections 9-10, SEP section 5, Fröhlich ch. 9), religion (Manifesto section 5, Fröhlich ch. 10), society and family (Manifesto section 7, Fröhlich ch. 8), world and imperialism (Manifesto section 11, Fröhlich ch. 8), economy (all sources). The movement's thinkers wrote little on economic policy: Fröhlich notes Tang never discussed capitalism or market economics, and Xu Fuguan's socialist sympathies and wish for land reform (s9) date from his political career before he became a Confucian scholar, so economic, ecological, technological and most world-policy statements stay null. Mou's and Xu's own political essays (e.g. Mou's Authority and Governance) were not available online in a citable copy.
